records.name: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS)
records.tldr: Cytokine release syndrome is systemic inflammation after immune activation, assessed through clinical findings and competing causes rather than a cytokine level alone.
records.summary:
Cytokine release syndrome can follow activation by engineered immune cells or T-cell-engaging treatments. Signals from several cell types can contribute to fever, hypotension, hypoxia and other organ effects. Infection or other conditions can produce similar findings or coexist with the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT consensus defines and grades CRS using attributed clinical findings, including fever at onset and the blood-pressure or oxygen support required. Its scale is a reporting framework, not a management algorithm. The 2026 ASTCT consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry; the numerical grading below is explicitly the 2019 version. Product, disease, preparation, observation window and treated denominator must accompany any incidence estimate.

notes: How CRS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. The definition requires a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher that cannot be attributed to another cause. Severity is then the more severe of two findings, again not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has neither. Grade 2 is low blood pressure that does not need vasopressors and/or oxygen by low-flow nasal cannula (up to 6 litres a minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 is one vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask or Venturi mask. Grade 4 is multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and/or positive pressure such as CPAP, BiPAP or intubation. Once someone has had a fever-lowering or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer needed to grade later severity: the grade then follows blood pressure and oxygen, and the person still counts as having CRS until the signs resolve. Organ toxicities linked to CRS are graded separately and do not change the CRS grade, and neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on the neurotoxicity scale, not added here. The 2026 ASTCT update (Perales et al.) convened experts to consider updating CRS, ICANS and haemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis-like grading, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it keeps, changes or relaxes any of these 2019 rules is not stated here; a report should say which version graded it.

Reading CRS without over-reading a cytokine level. CRS is a clinical syndrome, graded from attributed findings and not from a cytokine concentration. In a mouse model of CD19 CAR T-cell CRS, severity was mediated not by CAR T-cell-derived cytokines but by IL-6, IL-1 and nitric oxide from the recipient's macrophages, and IL-1 blockade abated it (Giavridis et al.); that supports a multicell amplification mechanism and does not show the same sources or shares in every human product. Infection and other conditions can cause or accompany the same findings, so the cause of a fever cannot be read from timing alone. A comparable report gives its grading version, observation window and treated denominator, with onset, maximum grade, interventions and resolution. Safety belongs to the product, disease, tumour burden and preparation, so experience with one blood-cancer product does not supply a solid-tumour product's rate, and no severe CRS in a small early study does not rule out uncommon events. CRS is a different problem from injury to healthy tissue that carries the target (on-target, off-tumour) and from neurotoxicity (ICANS). The treatment need not carry a cytokine payload to trigger endogenous inflammatory signalling. Tumour response does not establish acceptable inflammatory risk, and mild CRS does not establish lack of anticancer activity. Stopping a treatment input does not guarantee immediate removal of released signals or established injury. In a fictional early study, no severe CRS and a modest cytokine rise would not make every fever harmless CRS: attribution, clinical findings, a named grading framework, treated denominator and observation window are still needed.

Use the named consensus version when classifying immune-effector-cell toxicities. The 2026 ASTCT abstract describes updates to CRS, ICANS and IEC-HS and consensus work on haematotoxicity, non-ICANS neurologic events such as parkinsonism or cranial-nerve palsies, enterocolitis, tumour-inflammation-associated neurotoxicity and on-target off-tumour toxicity. It covers immune-effector-cell and T-cell-engager therapy. These category names do not diagnose an event from timing alone or supply the detailed grading criteria; clinical assessment still has to distinguish other causes. The absence of an added cytokine payload does not rule out inflammatory syndromes.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says almost everyone treated with engineered T-cell therapy has some level of cytokine release syndrome, that it most commonly develops within 10 days of the infusion, and that most cases are mild and easily treated. The signs it lists are fever and chills, a rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, low oxygen, headache, and feeling or being sick. Severe cases are treated with oxygen, fluids, steroids and tocilizumab, and usually improve within a few days. Around one person in five who has this treatment needs intensive care.

records.name: ICANS (neurotoxicity)
records.tldr: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome can affect language, attention, awareness or other brain functions; a cognitive score is one part of clinical assessment.
records.summary:
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, or ICANS, is a neurologic syndrome associated with immune-effector-cell therapy. Changes in language, attention, handwriting or awareness and more severe findings such as seizures need assessment against baseline and alternative explanations. An immune-marker plot does not establish the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT adult framework combines the immune effector cell-associated encephalopathy (ICE) score with consciousness, seizures, motor findings and raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema. Children require age-appropriate assessment. The 2026 consensus also addresses non-ICANS neurologic toxicities; its detailed tables were not accessible for this entry. Neurologic events and recovery need their own record rather than being inferred from resolution of CRS.

notes: How ICANS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. For adults, the grade is the most severe of five findings, none attributable to another cause. The 10-point ICE screen of orientation, naming, command-following, writing and attention scores 7 to 9 for grade 1, 3 to 6 for grade 2, 0 to 2 for grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable and cannot be tested for grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone who is awake with global aphasia can still be grade 3. Level of consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it: awakens spontaneously, awakens to voice, only to touch, or unarousable or requiring vigorous or repeated tactile stimulation. Any seizure that resolves rapidly, or EEG-only seizures that resolve with treatment, is grade 3, and prolonged (over 5 minutes) or repeated seizures without return to baseline are grade 4. Deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. Focal oedema on imaging is grade 3; diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad is grade 4; intracranial haemorrhage is excluded from ICANS grading. So ICE is a screen for encephalopathy and one input, not the whole examination: a person with an ICE of 3 who has a generalised seizure is grade 3, and headache alone is not a useful marker. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract adds categories such as non-ICANS neurological toxicities (parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsies, polyneuropathies) and tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity; their criteria, and any change to how ICE is used, were not readable here.

What is known about mechanism, timing and attribution. In 133 adults given CD19 CAR T cells, Gust et al. found that those with severe neurotoxicity had endothelial activation (disseminated intravascular coagulation, capillary leak) and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, and that the permeable barrier failed to protect the cerebrospinal fluid from high systemic cytokine concentrations including interferon-gamma. Higher risk went with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high marrow CD19-positive burden, high CAR T-cell dose, CRS and pre-existing neurological disease, and markers of endothelial activation before lymphodepletion were higher in people who later had grade 4 or worse neurotoxicity. That is an association in one product class and population, not a complete mechanism for every treatment. ICANS can accompany CRS or follow its own timetable, and neurotoxicity after CRS is scored separately, so recovery of blood pressure and oxygen does not show neurological recovery. If a person is confused while taking a sedating medicine and the ICE score falls, the grading rule requires that sedation be excluded, so the fall calls for clinical assessment, neither ignored nor diagnosed from the score alone. Clinical assessment also considers infection, metabolic disturbances, medicines and pre-existing neurologic disease. A safety report should retain onset, severity, attributed cause, interventions, duration, recovery and how many people were adequately observed. Separate fictional CRS and neurologic timelines can end at different times; they do not specify a typical order or duration. Stopping an engineered input does not guarantee immediate reversal of established neurologic injury.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says around one person in four treated with engineered T-cell therapy develops neurotoxicity, that it generally appears within 28 days of the infusion and often within a few days, and that symptoms are usually mild and resolve in a week or two. The signs it lists are confusion, speech problems, difficulty writing, headache and dizziness, shaking or tremor, and difficulty moving. Seizures and brain swelling are the serious forms. Someone who develops it is advised not to drive for 8 weeks from the onset of symptoms, and the requirement to have another adult present for the four weeks after infusion exists because the person affected is often the last to notice.

records.name: Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS: grading and management
records.tldr: Inflammatory and neurologic toxicities after immune-effector therapy need separate clinical assessment, grading and recovery records; the treatment plan depends on the product and findings.
records.summary:
The 2019 ASTCT consensus defines cytokine release syndrome using fever of at least 38°C not attributable to another cause. Its grade follows the more severe attributable hypotension or hypoxia criterion. Grade 1 has neither; grade 2 includes hypotension not requiring vasopressors or low-flow nasal oxygen or blow-by. Grade 3 includes one vasopressor with or without vasopressin, or high-flow nasal oxygen or a face mask. Grade 4 includes multiple vasopressors excluding vasopressin, or positive-pressure support. Once an individual with CRS receives fever-reducing or anti-cytokine treatment, fever is no longer needed to grade subsequent severity.

ICANS assessment is separate. In the adult 2019 framework, the ICE cognitive screen is combined with consciousness, seizures, motor findings and signs of raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema, excluding other causes. Improvement of blood pressure or oxygenation does not establish neurologic recovery.

The scale reports severity; it does not determine a universal treatment algorithm, preventive medicine or order of symptom onset. Management follows the clinical findings, product guidance and care team's protocol. Trial toxicity rates require their own grading version, population, denominator and follow-up. The 2026 consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry, so the numerical criteria here are explicitly historical 2019 criteria.

Perales et al., ASTCT consensus grading for toxicities after immune effector cell therapy (2026)

notes: ICANS grading in the 2019 ASTCT consensus: the grade is the most severe of the ICE score, level of consciousness, seizure, motor findings and raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema, none attributable to another cause. ICE 7 to 9 is grade 1, 3 to 6 grade 2, 0 to 2 grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone awake with global aphasia can be grade 3. Depressed consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it. Any clinical seizure, focal or generalised, that resolves rapidly, or non-convulsive seizures on EEG that resolve with intervention, is grade 3, while a life-threatening prolonged seizure (over 5 minutes), or repetitive clinical or electrical seizures without return to baseline in between, is grade 4; deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus do not change the ICANS grade; focal oedema is grade 3 and diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad grade 4, with intracranial haemorrhage excluded. Neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on this scale and not added to the CRS grade.

Version check: the grading above and in the summary is the ASTCT 2019 consensus. A 2026 ASTCT consensus on grading toxicities after immune effector cell therapy exists, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it changes the 2019 criteria is not stated here; use the version a trial states.

records.name: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV)
aka: Acute and delayed nausea and vomiting
records.tldr: Feeling or being sick after chemotherapy. Some drugs are far more likely to cause it than others, and the anti-sickness medicines given before treatment are chosen to match that risk, so most people are spared the worst of it.
records.summary: The MASCC/ESMO 2023 recommendations define the emetic risk of an intravenous anticancer drug as the risk of vomiting within the first 24 hours in patients given no antiemetic prophylaxis; high emetic risk means a risk of more than 90%, and includes cisplatin, carmustine, dacarbazine, mechlorethamine, streptozocin, cyclophosphamide above 1,500 mg/m² and anthracycline with cyclophosphamide in breast cancer. Trials score the acute phase (0 to 24 hours) and the delayed phase (24 to 120 hours) separately. Risk also depends on the patient (women and younger people are at higher risk) and on the prophylaxis given. For high-emetic-risk chemotherapy the guidelines recommend combinations of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, dexamethasone, an NK1 receptor antagonist and olanzapine. The ASCO 2020 update found no evidence to warrant omitting dexamethasone when checkpoint inhibitors are added to chemotherapy, and checkpoint inhibitors given without chemotherapy need no routine prophylaxis.

records.name: Antiemetics for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
records.tldr: Antiemetic medicines prevent or treat nausea and vomiting. The preventive plan depends on the treatment's emetic risk and the person's circumstances.
records.summary:
Antiemetic medicines are used to prevent or treat nausea and vomiting, which are separate outcomes. Options include serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists, dexamethasone and olanzapine. The regimen-specific guidance from MASCC and ESMO and the NCI PDQ describes combinations chosen for the emetic risk of the anticancer treatment and the clinical setting. A list of drug classes does not determine an individual medicine schedule.

Acute, delayed, anticipatory and breakthrough symptoms describe different timing or circumstances. Prevention differs from treatment of symptoms that have already appeared. Trials must state whether their endpoint is nausea, vomiting or a composite such as no vomiting and no rescue medication; meeting that composite does not establish that the person had no nausea.

notes: Nausea and vomiting are different outcomes. Nausea is the sensation and vomiting the expulsion; they often occur together but one can occur without the other. Serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors and substance P acting at NK1 receptors contribute with other transmitters, and in two phase II cisplatin studies serotonin appeared to dominate early vomiting and substance P the later phase, with overlap (Hesketh et al.), so acute and delayed are reporting windows and not sealed pathways. The NCI PDQ classes are acute (the first 24 hours after chemotherapy), delayed, anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory and chronic; anticipatory nausea was reported in about 29 per cent of patients and anticipatory vomiting in 11 per cent, with prevalence varying with definitions and methods. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.

Reading antiemetic trials. In Navari et al. (380 evaluable chemotherapy-naive adults given cisplatin at 70 mg per square metre or more, or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin, all with dexamethasone, an NK1 antagonist and a 5-HT3 antagonist), nausea prevention was the primary endpoint and complete response (no emesis and no rescue medication) a secondary one. No nausea in the first 24 hours was 74 per cent with olanzapine against 45 per cent with placebo, while complete response was 86 per cent against 65 per cent, so a complete response does not mean no nausea, and a person with no vomiting can still have persistent nausea. MASCC and ESMO updated their regimen-specific guideline in 2023 (Herrstedt et al., published 2024). Read patient-reported nausea severity, vomiting episodes, rescue-medication use and the observation window together with the preventive regimen and adherence; symptoms that limit drinking or eating warrant prompt contact with the care team. This describes how to read endpoints, not a medicine schedule.

Gut-to-brain nerve signalling, blood-borne inputs and learned associations can contribute, so one blocked route does not account for every symptom. The timing terms organise observations. Acute commonly refers to the first 24 hours, delayed to symptoms beyond 24 hours, anticipatory to symptoms before treatment associated with previous experiences, and breakthrough to symptoms despite prevention. Learned symptoms are real; delayed does not mean mild, and early and later responses can overlap with multiday treatment. Prevention and treatment of symptoms that have appeared are different questions. In a fictional trial, no vomiting and no rescue medicine can meet its complete-response endpoint while the participant still reports nausea. Relief of either symptom does not measure tumour response.
records.principle: Prevention is matched to the regimen's emetogenic risk and patient factors. Medicines act on overlapping signalling pathways, including serotonin, substance P and dopamine; acute and delayed describe observation windows rather than exclusive mechanisms.
strengths: Complete response in ~70-80% even with cisplatin
limitations: Delayed and anticipatory nausea still common
Olanzapine sedation; dexamethasone and immunotherapy interactions

records.name: Insertional mutagenesis
records.tldr: Insertional mutagenesis is a change in a cell's genes caused by added genetic material landing in its DNA and disrupting a gene or its control, and neither an insertion nor a growing cell clone shows by itself that a cancer has formed or what caused it.
records.summary:
Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

What regulators ask for follows from this. The ABECMA prescribing information revised in November 2025 carries a boxed warning that T-cell malignancies, including CAR-positive tumours, have occurred after BCMA- and CD19-directed genetically modified autologous T-cell immunotherapies for blood cancers, may present within weeks of infusion and may be fatal, and says to monitor life-long for secondary malignancies. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance recommends following people for 15 years after treatment with CAR T cells containing an integrated transgene, because integrating vectors may increase the risk of delayed adverse events and non-integrating vectors are thought to carry a low delayed risk. These are class-level product warnings and follow-up expectations; they do not assign one mechanism to every event or give an incidence for other products.

To attribute a malignancy after engineered-cell therapy, investigators ask whether the therapeutic sequence is present in the malignant cells, where the integrations are, whether they alter relevant genes, whether related clones were detectable earlier, and what prior therapy, underlying disease and pre-existing genetic changes contribute. Integration-site sequencing maps insertion locations, quantitative DNA assays estimate vector copies per cell, and flow cytometry, gene-expression measurement and pathology answer different questions about identity, function and malignancy; the sample is consumed by testing. Average vector copy number cannot show the position or effect of each insertion, a clone's frequency depends on the sampled cells, assay sensitivity and time, and blood may not represent every tissue. This record gives no copy-number or clone-frequency threshold because none of the sources read sets one. Messenger RNA delivery that does not integrate does not use genomic insertion as its route, which does not remove its other risks.

notes: In a fictional follow-up example, an engineered-cell clone becomes more common but no new malignancy has been established. The observation prompts examination of the clone, insertion sites, gene effects and clinical findings. A growth pattern, a malignant diagnosis and an insertion-driven mechanism are separate claims. An insertion that leaves no demonstrated gene effect, one that interrupts a gene and one that alters nearby regulation are different possibilities; none of those schematic locations assigns an incidence or time to cancer. A CAR-positive malignancy can establish product ancestry without identifying which change drove it.

Hamilton’s secondary T-cell-lymphoma case followed axicabtagene ciloleucel. The NCI Drug Dictionary describes that product’s gammaretroviral vector; it should not be relabelled as a lentiviral product. The study found no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration in the deeply profiled case. Product identity, the diagnosis and investigation of its cause remain separate; that finding does not negate the malignancy warning or estimate the risk of every other integrating system.

records.name: On-target, off-tumour toxicity and off-target cross-reactivity
records.tldr: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is harm to healthy tissue that carries the same target a treatment was built to recognise, so accurate recognition injures the tissue as well as the cancer.
records.summary:
On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. The authors hypothesised that highly active ERBB2-directed T cells recognised ERBB2 on normal lung cells on first pass through the lung and released inflammatory cytokines that began a cascade ending in multiorgan failure; the autopsy findings were read as initial lung injury followed by days of hypotension and ischaemia, and the authors call the significance of the cells' reactivity against cultured primary cells unclear. This is a single case, with a stated dose and conditioning, whose mechanism is the authors' hypothesis and which gives no incidence for any CAR product (Morgan et al., 2010). In a trial of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor against HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3 in myeloma and melanoma, the first two patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days; no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and beating cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells triggered T-cell killing through recognition of an unrelated peptide from titin. That is off-target recognition of an unintended molecule, not the intended target in the wrong tissue (Linette et al., 2013).

How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. In practice a readout is a staining intensity or positive fraction, a binding profile, killing or cytokine release by healthy cells at a named time, and finally organ injury in the treated population; stained fixed tissue does not show a living organ's accessibility, an animal model may lack the human target, and a negative result in one panel is not a safety certificate. No universal expression cut-off is given here because no source read gives one. Whether affinity tuning, recognition logic or control switches improve safety for a particular design needs that design's own evidence. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

notes: A fictional receptor kills X-positive tumour cells and normal airway cells that also display X: that is the on-target, off-tumour problem. If it also recognises Y on an X-negative healthy cell, that is off-target cross-reactivity. Binding or surface contact does not itself measure injury. Record tissue, assay sensitivity, staining intensity, positive fraction or calibrated molecules per cell, binding specificity, and healthy-cell killing or cytokine release at a named time; viable-cell tests consume the sample. Clinical organ injury is a further outcome in the actual population and regimen. A staining ratio, one negative panel or a control switch does not establish safety everywhere or guarantee reversal of an injury already present.

In a fictional tumour sample, 70 of 100 cells display an epitope accessible to the proposed receptor and 30 do not. A second target has only an RNA result, while healthy tissue was stained with a third antibody. Those measurements cannot rank safe receptor designs: ask for the actual binder’s recognition, the unrecognised tumour population and functional effects on relevant healthy cells. A more sensitive receptor might recognise additional tumour cells and additional healthy cells. Even a perfectly specific binder can harm healthy cells carrying its intended antigen; unintended binding to another molecule is a different failure. A sampled panel can miss antigen-negative cells, and an intracellular signal does not establish an accessible surface epitope. Repeat the relevant healthy-cell question under conditions, including inflammation, that could change recognition.

records.name: What it costs to aim at a lineage antigen
records.tldr: Some lymphoma treatments recognise lineage antigens shared with healthy cells. Those normal-cell targets can explain particular harms; cytokine-mediated effects and unintended binding are different mechanisms.
records.summary:
Nearly all the surface targets in lymphoma are what the corpus calls lineage antigens: normal proteins on a normal cell type, present on the cancer because the cancer came from that cell type. Only a few, such as CD30, are close to restricted to activated cells in an adult. This has consequences that can be read off the target before the first dose.

CD20 and CD19 are on every normal B cell, so anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 treatments empty the B-cell compartment. What follows is low immunoglobulin, more bacterial and viral infection, a blunted response to vaccination, and, specifically, reactivation of hepatitis B, which is why surface antigen and core antibody are checked before the first dose of rituximab. After CAR-T the aplasia is deeper and longer, sometimes years, and immunoglobulin replacement is part of the plan rather than a rescue.

CD52 is on B cells, T cells, monocytes and dendritic cells, so alemtuzumab produces the most profound lymphopenia of any antibody used in lymphoma, with CD4 counts that can stay low for a year, and with it cytomegalovirus reactivation, Pneumocystis pneumonia and fungal infection.

CCR4 is on regulatory T cells as well as on the tumour, so mogamulizumab removes the cells that hold autoimmunity in check: rash is common, and giving it shortly before an allogeneic transplant has been associated with severe graft-versus-host disease.

CD47 is on red cells, where its job is to tell a macrophage not to eat them, so blocking it causes anaemia by design; the dosing strategy that made the class usable is a low priming dose followed by higher maintenance doses.

CD38 produces a laboratory problem rather than a clinical one: anti-CD38 antibodies bind CD38 on red cells and make the indirect antiglobulin test positive, masking real alloantibodies, so the transfusion laboratory must be warned before a crossmatch.

CD3 is not a lineage antigen of the tumour in B-cell disease: it is the handle a T-cell-engaging bispecific antibody uses to grip a T cell. The cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity that can follow come from immune-cell activation, a systemic inflammatory mechanism that is distinct from injury to a healthy cell carrying the target, and they are graded separately (ASTCT) and reduced in practice with step-up dosing.

records.name: Lymphodepletion before CAR-T
records.tldr: Lymphodepletion reduces existing lymphocytes before some cell therapies. It changes the immune environment; the medicines, timing and need for it depend on the treatment protocol.
records.summary: Lymphodepletion removes regulatory T cells and cytokine sinks, raising IL-7 and IL-15 levels so infused CAR-T cells proliferate; its intensity correlates with expansion, response and also toxicity. Fludarabine shortages led to bendamustine substitution with similar outcomes. It causes a week or two of cytopenias and infection risk and contributes to prolonged cytopenias after CAR-T. In vivo CAR-T approaches and some allogeneic products aim to work without lymphodepletion, which would remove a major barrier to outpatient and community delivery. Vein-to-vein time includes the wait for manufacturing before lymphodepletion can begin.

links.label: Wikipedia
Gattinoni et al., removal of homeostatic cytokine sinks by lymphodepletion (2005)
Rohaan et al., tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy or ipilimumab in advanced melanoma (2022)
NCI: T-cell transfer therapy and preparation before cell infusion

notes: Why preparing the body can help transferred cells, and what it costs. In mouse adoptive-transfer experiments, a nonmyeloablative regimen enhanced antitumour effect even without regulatory T cells, through greater function of tumour-reactive CD8-positive T cells rather than greater numbers; interleukin-7 and interleukin-15 were required, and removing endogenous cells that respond to those cytokines reproduced the effect, which points to lymphodepletion removing cells that act as cytokine sinks (Gattinoni et al.). That is a mouse mechanism and it does not describe an empty physical space. When a trial tests conditioning, transferred cells and cytokine support together, the outcomes belong to the whole package: in the phase 3 tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte trial in advanced melanoma (Rohaan et al.; 168 patients, 86 per cent with disease refractory to anti-PD-1 treatment), cells were infused after nonmyeloablative cyclophosphamide plus fludarabine and followed by high-dose interleukin-2, and grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in all patients given TILs, mainly chemotherapy-related myelosuppression. Nonmyeloablative therefore does not mean harmless.

Counts need their denominators. A percentage of white cells is not an absolute count: with invented numbers, 20 per cent of 2,000 white cells per microlitre is 400 lymphocytes, and a later 40 per cent of 500 is 200, so the fraction doubled while the count halved. Lymphocyte and neutrophil counts are separate measurements, cytopenia means a low count of any blood cell type, and none of these measures tumour killing.

Lymphocytes include T cells, B cells and natural killer cells. Preparation can affect competition, regulation and, for donor products, host rejection; it can also act on cancer directly. It does not create a missing tumour antigen or guarantee that transferred cells enter a solid tumour. The need for preparation and its recovery criteria belong to the named protocol, rather than to every cell therapy. Serial blood counts consume blood samples rather than tumour tissue. Report absolute lymphocytes and neutrophils with units, sampling time and reference ranges, and measure transferred-cell number, location and function separately from the counts. More depletion is not automatically more benefit. Nonmyeloablative describes a regimen not intended to eliminate marrow blood production completely, rather than a promise of mild count suppression. Report severity, duration, recovery, infections, organ harms and relevant support with the regimen. More transferred cells, more depletion and more tumour killing are separate propositions.

records.name: Neutropenia
records.tldr: Neutropenia means a low concentration of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell that helps fight infection. The count, how long it stays low and the treatment context matter; a low count alone does not establish infection.
records.summary: The commonest dose-limiting toxicity of cytotoxic chemotherapy and of several targeted drugs (CDK4/6 inhibitors, PARP inhibitors, sacituzumab govitecan) and cell therapies. Graded by absolute neutrophil count (CTCAE v5.0: grade 3 <1.0, grade 4 <0.5 × 10⁹/L; CTCAE v6.0 of 2025 moved these to grade 3 <0.5 and grade 4 <0.1 × 10⁹/L); severity and duration determine infection risk and febrile neutropenia. Managed by dose delays and reductions, prophylactic G-CSF, and for some drugs (palbociclib) simply tolerated because it is uncomplicated. Trilaciclib protects marrow during chemotherapy in small-cell lung cancer. Prolonged cytopenias after CAR-T (ICAHT) and after lymphodepletion are distinct in mechanism and can last months.

notes: Reading a neutrophil count. The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the number of neutrophils per volume of blood, written as cells per microlitre or as times 10 to the ninth per litre; it is more specific than the total white cell count, which includes other cell types. One ANC is a snapshot. Two invented curves make the point: both read 0.5 times 10 to the ninth per litre on day 3, but in one the count dips briefly and recovers, while in the other it stays at that level from day 2 to day 4. The matching number does not mean matching risk, because depth, duration and trend matter, and a count alone neither establishes nor excludes infection. Keep the sampling date, units, the laboratory's reference range and the place in the treatment cycle with the number. NCI patient guidance lists a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher among the signs of infection to report promptly, whatever an earlier count showed. Better counts and fewer infections are related but separate outcomes, and neither is tumour response.

For a prevention study, retain the actual anticancer regimen, risk factors, comparator, fever-and-count definition and observation window. A toxicity report needs its count threshold and grading version. The same ANC on one date can conceal different durations of low counts, and an earlier reassuring count does not dismiss new fever or other infection symptoms. Supportive-care benefit, such as fewer infections, is distinct from cancer control.

Carboplatin-paclitaxel, anthracycline chemotherapy and sacituzumab govitecan all lower white cells; NICE NG101 notes neutropenic sepsis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia are more frequent with platinum-based chemotherapy. Macmillan says a minor infection can become life-threatening within hours when neutrophils are low, to buy a thermometer, and to ring the 24-hour helpline for a temperature over 37.5 C or below 36 C, or for feeling unwell even with a normal temperature.

Breast Cancer Now says growth factor injections are sometimes recommended with sacituzumab govitecan to reduce the risk of infection; NICE CG151 says G-CSF is not routine for everyone but is used where a regimen needs it or to keep the dose on time.

FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX and gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel all lower white cells. Macmillan says to ring the 24-hour number straight away for a temperature above 37.5 C or below 36 C, or for feeling unwell even with a normal temperature; blood counts are checked before each dose and treatment is delayed if they are low.

FOLFOX, CAPOX, FOLFIRI and irinotecan all lower white cells. Macmillan says to contact the hospital straight away on the 24-hour number for a temperature outside the range your team gave you, shivering, or feeling unwell even with a normal temperature; blood counts are checked before each cycle and treatment is delayed when they are low.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says a neutrophil count below 1 billion per litre is generally classed as neutropenia, that the reference range is usually 2 to 7.5 billion per litre, and that ranges differ between people and between ethnic groups, with people of African, Caribbean, Middle Eastern and West Indian descent often having naturally lower counts without a higher infection risk. It says there is limited scientific research supporting a neutropenic diet and that advice varies between hospitals, so the team's own instructions are the ones to follow.

records.name: Growth factors: G-CSF and febrile neutropenia prevention
records.tldr: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor medicines support neutrophil production and recovery. Their use depends on the treatment regimen, infection risk and individual clinical context.
records.summary:
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor medicines support neutrophil production in selected clinical settings. They have a different job from the treatment directed at the cancer. Filgrastim acts through receptors on relevant blood-forming cells; it does not replace all missing blood-cell types or create immediate general immunity.

The 2026 ASCO update supports primary prophylaxis when a chemotherapy regimen's febrile-neutropenia risk is approximately 20% or higher and no equally effective and safe alternative not requiring it is available. Below 20%, age, history or disease characteristics can still justify prophylaxis. Those recommendations require the named regimen and individual clinical context; they do not make every low neutrophil count an indication for treatment. Product, schedule, monitoring and management of fever belong to the care team's plan.

notes: What the 2026 ASCO update says. Prophylactic colony-stimulating factors to reduce febrile neutropenia are warranted when the chemotherapy regimen's risk is approximately 20 per cent or higher and no equally effective and safe regimen without them exists, and may be warranted below 20 per cent when age, medical history or disease characteristics put a patient at high risk; it also covers stem-cell mobilisation with plerixafor or motixafortide and newer products and biosimilars (Gyawali et al., abstract; systematic review of 33 randomised trials and 16 systematic reviews searched to August 2025). The authors' slide set gives the population as adults with solid tumours or hematologic malignancies treated with systemic antineoplastic therapy, where the JCO abstract says adults with cancer, and neither covers children. The recommendations depend on regimen and individual risk; they do not make every low count an indication for a growth factor.

What the drug does and what it does not. Colony-stimulating factors act on haematopoietic cells by binding specific cell-surface receptors and stimulating proliferation, differentiation commitment and some end-cell functional activation; endogenous G-CSF is lineage specific and regulates neutrophil production in the marrow (filgrastim prescribing information). It supports neutrophil recovery and does not supply a complete immune system, boost antitumour immunity or replace other blood cells. Bone pain is a labelled adverse reaction; its frequency belongs to the particular study population and regimen. The label also warns about uncommon serious harms, including splenic rupture and acute respiratory distress syndrome, and reports MDS or AML in patients with breast or lung cancer receiving chemotherapy and/or radiation. These warnings do not supply an individual probability. Supportive-care benefit, such as a better count or fewer infections, is not tumour response. Shorter- and longer-acting preparations have product-specific delivery and monitoring requirements; a class name does not select a product, amount or schedule.
records.principle: Recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor accelerates neutrophil precursor proliferation and release, shortening the neutropenic nadir after myelosuppressive chemotherapy.
strengths: Halves febrile neutropenia; maintains dose intensity
limitations: Bone pain is a recognised adverse reaction; its rate depends on the product and setting.
Cost and access can affect delivery of supportive care.

Serious filgrastim label warnings include splenic rupture and acute respiratory distress syndrome; the label also addresses monitoring for myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia in people with breast or lung cancer receiving chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.

records.name: Filgrastim (G-CSF)
records.tldr: Filgrastim (Neupogen and its biosimilars) is a daily injection that speeds the recovery of infection-fighting white cells after chemotherapy, lets doctors give chemotherapy on schedule and mobilises stem cells for transplant.
records.summary: Filgrastim was approved by the FDA in February 1991 to reduce the incidence of infection from febrile neutropenia in non-myeloid malignancies receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy, and later for AML induction, bone marrow transplantation, peripheral blood progenitor cell mobilisation, severe chronic neutropenia and acute radiation syndrome. It was the first Amgen blockbuster and the model for supportive-care biologics; the first US biosimilar of any kind was filgrastim-sndz (Zarxio, 2015), and the EU authorised the first filgrastim biosimilars in 2008. Guidelines recommend primary prophylaxis when the febrile neutropenia risk of a regimen exceeds about 20%. Bone pain is the main adverse effect; splenic rupture, acute respiratory distress syndrome and sickle cell crises are rare but serious. Pegfilgrastim gives a once-per-cycle alternative.

records.name: Febrile neutropenia
records.tldr: Fever in a patient whose infection-fighting white cells have been wiped out by chemotherapy. It is a medical emergency: without immune cells, an ordinary infection can become fatal in hours, so antibiotics are started immediately.
records.summary: Defined as temperature ≥38.3°C (or ≥38.0°C sustained) with neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, it occurs in 10-20% of patients on standard chemotherapy regimens (higher with docetaxel-based, dose-dense and induction chemotherapy), carries 5-10% mortality and is a leading cause of unplanned admission. Management is empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within an hour, risk-scored (MASCC) to allow oral outpatient treatment for low-risk cases. Prevention with G-CSF (filgrastim, pegfilgrastim) is recommended when a regimen's risk exceeds 20%, and febrile neutropenia is a standard dose-limiting toxicity and reason for dose reduction.

notes: Fever with neutropenia is defined by a stated temperature and a stated neutrophil threshold, which a trial or guideline should name. A low count alone does not establish infection, and infection can occur without neutropenia, so the count and the fever are separate findings that together define the syndrome and prompt assessment before any source of infection is found.

Triple-negative breast cancer: the NHS says call 999 or go to A&E if an adult is breathing very fast, is confused or slurring, has blue, pale or blotchy skin, has a very high or very low temperature or is shivery, or has a rash that does not fade when pressed, and not to drive yourself. Macmillan's earlier signs to ring the 24-hour line: temperature over 37.5 C or below 36 C, shivering, or symptoms of a urine, chest, skin or tooth infection.

Pancreatic cancer chemotherapy: the NHS says call 999 or go to A&E for breathing very fast, confusion or slurred speech, blue, pale or blotchy skin, a very high or very low temperature, shivering, or a rash that does not fade when pressed. A blocked bile duct or stent is a second route to sepsis in this cancer, so fever counts even when the blood count is normal.

Bowel cancer chemotherapy: the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for breathing very fast, confusion or slurred speech, blue, pale or blotchy skin, a very high or very low temperature, shivering, or a rash that does not fade when pressed. A stoma is a second route to dehydration and infection in this cancer, so fever with a high stoma output counts twice.

Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says a common sign of neutropenic sepsis is a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, and that it is possible to have neutropenic sepsis without a fever, sometimes called cold sepsis, which steroid treatment makes more likely because steroids can mask a fever. For that reason teams also use heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate and kidney and liver function to check for it. Steroids are part of almost every lymphoma regimen, so the no-fever presentation is not a rarity here.

records.name: Cytopenias and myelosuppression
records.tldr: The umbrella term for low blood counts of any kind (white cells, red cells, platelets) when treatment suppresses the bone marrow. Most chemotherapy causes it temporarily; radioligands, CAR-T and some pills cause longer-lasting versions.
records.summary: Myelosuppression is the shared toxicity of cytotoxic chemotherapy, conditioning regimens, lymphodepletion, radioligand therapy (177Lu-PSMA, PRRT) and a range of targeted agents, graded per lineage by CTCAE; pancytopenia means all three lineages are low. Blood counts before each cycle gate treatment, and delays and dose reductions are the standard responses. After CAR-T, prolonged and biphasic cytopenias (ICAHT) affect a third of patients and drive infection deaths months after infusion; lymphopenia is a marker of poorer immunotherapy outcomes. Therapy-related MDS is the late, permanent form of marrow injury.

records.name: Cellular kinetics and persistence
records.tldr: A living cell therapy can change its number, location and state after administration. The starting dose, a sampled cell count and useful function are different measurements.
records.summary: After a cell infusion, measured abundance depends on division, survival and redistribution. In vivo engineering may also continue to generate newly engineered cells. A blood sample describes one compartment and time; it cannot count all cells in the body or establish entry into a tumor. Detectable receptor-encoding sequences, viable receptor-positive cells, persistent markers and functional activity should be reported separately.

notes: FDA CAR T-cell guidance treats exposure/kinetics, pharmacodynamic response, immunogenicity, identity, viability and potency as distinct assessments. Blood concentration-time measurements and optional disease-tissue sampling answer different distribution questions. A sequence assay is not automatically a count of viable cells expressing a functional surface receptor.

Keep the measurement method, time, compartment, units and denominator attached. A receptor-positive percentage can fall while absolute receptor-positive cells per microliter remain unchanged if the sampled denominator increases. Neither measure alone establishes an unchanged total-body cell population, tumor entry or antitumor benefit.

An administered cell dose is an input. The dose of a vector or particle used for in vivo engineering does not directly specify the later number of engineered cells. Autologous means the recipient’s own cells; allogeneic means cells from another person. Engineering outside versus inside the body is a separate axis; a prepared delivery product can engineer the recipient's own cells.

Expansion and persistence can prolong useful activity or harmful recognition. Stopping further administration does not instantly remove living cells or reverse an injury already triggered. A safety switch addresses a specified control mechanism; cell elimination, receptor shutoff and treatment of downstream inflammation are different interventions.

In the Liu cord-blood CAR-NK study, low-level detection at least 12 months after treatment belonged to a construct with IL-15 and an inducible caspase-9 switch. It does not establish the behavior of every NK-cell source or equate marker detection with continuing useful function.

In a fictional pair of matched blood samples, 20 per cent of 100 viable T cells per microlitre and 10 per cent of 200 both give 20 receptor-positive viable T cells per microlitre. The percentage fell because its denominator doubled; the concentration did not. This conclusion requires comparable collection, volume and viable-cell gates. It says nothing about the total number of cells in the body, tumour entry or continued target-cell killing. Genetic copies, surface receptor, viable cells and useful function remain separate measurements.

Cells respond biologically to signals, without intention; more cells do not by themselves establish better or safer treatment. Consider two fictional ready-made products: a carrier that gives receptor instructions to the recipient’s own T cells, and a prepared batch of donor-derived engineered cells. The first can generate autologous cells in vivo; the second supplies allogeneic cells engineered ex vivo. State four things separately: the starting cell family, whose cells they are, where engineering happens and whether cells or an instruction carrier are administered. Neither card establishes available supply, the final engineered-cell population or treatment benefit. NK and NKT name different cell families; an added receptor does not erase the recipient cell’s other inputs.

A rise in engineered cells in blood with few found in two tumour biopsies leaves distribution and infiltration unresolved. Blood abundance is not entry into a mass of tissue, and a biopsy represents its sampled place and time. If a receptor works in a simple culture but killing falls in a more complex model with the target still present, investigate access, cell state and the model’s other features with controlled perturbations. The contrast alone does not identify a macrophage, vessel or signalling pathway as the cause, or show that more expansion will solve it. Expression of PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3 or TIGIT, or a count of macrophages or suppressor cells, does not by itself establish which input caused the functional difference. Trafficking toward a site and infiltration into tissue are different steps, and vessel number does not measure perfusion. Chronic stimulation, low oxygen, limited nutrients and inhibitory signals are different hypotheses; exhaustion describes cell states rather than physical tiredness.

Compare time courses rather than labels when interpreting reversibility. Antibodies also take time to clear after dosing stops. In an engineered-cell product, carrier exposure, instructions, receptor protein, living cells and inflammation can have different durations. Stopping the next administration, reducing one signal, removing the cells and reversing an established injury are separate claims.
